https://hungarytoday.hu/the-democratic-r.text: “The Democratic Rule of Law has Ceased to Exist” as President Signs Constitutional Amendment Tamás Sulyok signed the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, automatically ending his own term as President of the Republic tomorrow. With the amendment’s removal of almost all other checks and balances, Hungary will effectively cease to be a democracy. In addition to the removal of the President of the Republic and the President of the Constitutional Court, a term limit for members of parliament will take effect, barring most of the opposition in parliament from running in the 2030 parliamentary elections. In the video published on his social media platform, President Tamás Sulyok said that the Hungarian people are a wonderful people, a strong and great nation of Europe who have already endured numerous hardships, but in every struggle, have been able to rely on solid pillars. One such solid pillar stems from the development of Hungarian law, which rests on a thousand-year-old foundation. The rule of law means, above all, respect for the law—that is, the supremacy of the law over arbitrariness, and the supremacy of legal norms over individual decisions by public authorities—said the outgoing president. He stated that if the politicization of power circumvents the limits of the law, it will have unforeseeable consequences for our country.” In his view, this is a serious case in a constitutional sense and an unprecedented one in the 36 years of Hungarian democracy since the transition to democracy. Sulyok noted that the Hungarian National Assembly had voted to adopt the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law. This amendment terminates the term of office of the incumbent President of the Republic with a single sentence. This sentence joins the ranks of those forced Gordian knots that will remain for posterity as grave and shameful historical examples of the abuse of political power,” he stated. Sulyok expressed the view that the primary responsibility of state institutions and the chief representatives of state power is mutual respect and the cooperation based on it. That is why he did not resign from the office of head of state. In his view, this means, above all, respect for human dignity in interpersonal relationships, and, in relations between institutions, respect for each other’s constitutional roles and powers. Only in this way can every state body fulfill its own constitutional role and mission. These principles also form the foundation of a civilized system of government based on the rule of law, in keeping with European culture. He believes that it is contrary to these principles for public authorities to seek to achieve their goals through threats, the exertion of pressure, and the circumvention of constitutional rules. “In response to messages demanding my resignation and threatening my removal, the protection of the constitutional order and the authority of the office of the head of state left me with only one course of action: to remain in office,” he stated. The 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law marked a breaking point in Hungarian constitutional democracy. By removing public officials—an act that openly violates the rule of law and the independence of institutions—and by imposing unprecedented restrictions on the right to vote, it sets a negative precedent that inflicts a deep wound on the constitutional values of democracy, the separation of powers, and the rule of law —emphasized Sulyok. He stated that the rule of law is fundamental to him, and that as president, he has always carried out his duties within the framework of the Fundamental Law and with full respect for it. As he noted, the foremost evidence of this is that the new ruling party has consistently viewed amending the Fundamental Law as the only way to remove him from office. Sulyok stated that we have reached a crossroads regarding a matter of national importance that transcends personal or political interests. In such a case, the president has two options: to fulfill his constitutional duty by signing the bill, or to refuse to sign it—which, however, would constitute a violation of the law. He announced that, under the current Fundamental Law, there is no constitutional remedy available against this amendment—which violates constitutional principles but was adopted by the National Assembly, as the body empowered to amend the Constitution, through a lawful procedure. “The sole responsibility for this decision lies with those who have the power to amend the Constitution.” Photo: Facebook Péter Magyar “I am fulfilling my obligation enshrined in the Fundamental Law after thoroughly weighing my legal options and my conscience. My signature is the final seal of my obligations as President of the Republic and of my complete and unconditional respect for the office of the President of the Republic under all circumstances. It is a sign that I have upheld Hungary’s Fundamental Law throughout and have not violated it,” he stated. He went on to add that it is also enduring proof that the fundamental values of a free society—the rule of law, democracy, and the principle of the separation of powers—have been trampled upon for the sake of power. The sole responsibility for this decision lies with those who have the power to amend the Constitution.” The democratic rule of law that emerged from the legacy of 1956 at the time of the regime change has thus ceased to exist —declared Sulyok. He went on to say that the legitimacy of the president of the Republic, which had remained unchanged since the transition to democracy, has also ceased to exist. Hungary’s next head of state will, in fact, replace a president who was removed through a process that violated constitutional values. He emphasized that the office of the president of the Republic will become subservient to the executive branch and politics; its role under public law will fade, and its fundamental function will cease to exist. Furthermore, it will no longer serve as any kind of check or balance. Those who stand firm in their faith and in the truth do not resort to violence, do not revile others, and do not humiliate others in their dignity. I believe that remaining human and humane, true to ourselves and to the truth, despite all attacks and under all circumstances, is the only path worth choosing. Let us cherish all that unites us; let us love Hungary—said the outgoing president in closing. Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán reacted to the news with a post saying: Today, the last barrier has fallen. Tyranny is no longer a threat, but a reality. If this could be done to the President of the Republic, then tomorrow no one will be safe. May God protect Hungary!” The prime minister signaled stricter conflict-of-interest rules. Photograph: SAUDI PRESS AGENCY/AFP/Getty Images Middle East and north Africa Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in Yemen Relations between the two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudi Arabia in Yemen Patrick Wintour Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.52 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 12.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates over Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back. Relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia in Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which it had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently effectively quit Yemen. But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthi drive to the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait against pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed. The future role of the UAE in Yemen was discussed at a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday attended by the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, UAE president Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan and a group of other Arab states, including representatives of Saudi Arabia. 2:34 Why the civil war in Yemen has world governments on edge Netanyahu reportedly offered to help Saudi Arabia defeat the Houthis , an offer that Riyadh would probably find near impossible to accept, even though Donald Trump has failed to answer the Saudi call for US help in Yemen. A further meeting to discuss Yemen took place on Tuesday in Riyadh between Prince Khalid bin Salman al Saud, the Saudi defence minister, and Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE vice president. It is part of a range of signs from the two sides suggesting they may want to find a path to reconciliation, even if only on energy. Following the Houthi push to the Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint on Saudi oil exports, its forces are now trying to consolidate their gains and take the south-western city of Taiz. “The Houthi forces are mounting simultaneous waves of attacks on the city trying to exhaust the Taiz Axis force defending the city. The Houthis are pushed back, but then the next day they come again on a different front,” said Baraa Shiban, a Gulf and Yemen specialist at the defence think tank Rusi who has just spent a week in Taiz. “Efforts are being made to try to end the rift between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and there may be some confidence-building measures. But the UAE has left Yemen, and it is unlikely that Riyadh would let them back in since they are aligned with the STC, and that would spell trouble … the UAE and Saudi Arabia are fundamentally on opposite sides.” The STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, fled into exile following the Saudi attack on its forces and the movement became marginalised as a political force. But the former Yemen foreign minister and STC supporter Khaled Alyemany told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia may have to reconsider its political approach to the southern issue since the Giant Brigades, the UAE-trained southern forces once associated with the STC, provide some of the most reliable, well-equipped forces on the ground to stem the Houthi advance. The Giant Brigades, however, have been urged by the STC to resist merging with Yemen government forces, arguing to do so will set back the separatist cause. “We cannot fight and wage wars in the north against the Houthis if we do not have a horizon for our independence,” Alyemany said. “The UN recognised government … operating from exile in Riyadh, insists that southerners fight to retake the capital, Sana’a, on its behalf, but without any promise of the south’s right to self-determination,” he said. “The problem is so long as the Yemen government derives its legitimacy from its Saudi funders rather than its people, the outcome is not Saudi Arabia’s stated goal of security along its southern borders.” The White House has also been privately urging the UAE and the Saudi to bury their differences and allow a unified military command including the Southern Giants Brigades to challenge the Houthi advance. An additional proposal is to use Israeli intelligence and hire Israeli private security firms, something the UAE has done sometimes to brutal effect in the past in Yemen. Saudi Arabia, reluctant to be seen cooperating with Israel, has also always resisted helping the southern separatists since division of the country might entrench Houthi rule in the north along its border. The Houthis have used drones and missiles to attack Saudi energy installations. Despite Saudi air cover and support, the current battle to prevent the Houthis consolidating their gains is such that the parliament of the UN-recognised government has sanctioned a general mobilisation of the Yemeni people to fight the Houthis. The World Health Organization stated that 838 people were killed and 3,643 others were injured due to the recent escalation in Yemen from 6 August last year until 26 September this year. The Houthis insist they are not seeking to block general commercial shipping in the strait, but only that linked to Saudi Arabia. On Monday it published figures showing commercial shipping was flowing as normal. The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia is in effect a colonial power, and the UN-recognised government based in Aden is a creature of Riyadh with no independent ability to govern the country. April Longley Alley, senior fellow at Washington Institute, told an International Crisis Group seminar that the war is existential for the Saudis, but the Houthis are not going to compromise. “We will have to see if they hold these territories, but what the Houthis learned from the Iran war is that Saudi under pressure and attack will seek de-escalation,” she said. “The Houthis are demanding a victor’s peace.” Explore more on these topics Middle East and north Africa Yemen Houthis Saudi Arabia United Arab Emirates news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://english.news.cn/20260920/72f8b35.text: Feature: From sea route to global supply chains, shipping company charts China's trade growth Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-20 19:00:45 A drone photo taken on May 22, 2026 shows a new vessel of Chipolbrok, a Chinese-Polish Joint Stock Shipping Company, docking at Taicang Port in east China's Jiangsu Province. (Chipolbrok/Handout via Xinhua) GDYNIA, Poland, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Over 20 years in shipping, Li Zhiping has witnessed the change of both the cargoes and trade patterns around him. When he started out as a seafarer, most of the ships he worked on sailed from Europe to China or South America. China-bound vessels often carried machinery and technical equipment from Europe. About a decade ago, Li began to notice the change of direction of cargo flows -- more voyages were starting in China. Today, as a shipping division director, he sees Chinese-made wind power equipment, transformers and energy storage units on cargo lists bound for Europe, the United States, Australia and the Middle East. The shift Li has observed over the course of his career reflects a broader change in China's trade with the world. The company he works for, Chipolbrok, a Chinese-Polish Joint Stock Shipping Company, offers a longer view of that change. Founded by China and Poland in 1951, it was the first Sino-foreign joint venture established in the People's Republic of China. In its early years, ships on the route carried machinery, steel and other equipment urgently needed for China's industrial development. More than seven decades later, both the scale and composition of China's trade look very different. According to customs statistics, China's goods trade reached a record 45.47 trillion yuan (about 6.8 trillion U.S. dollars) in 2025, up 3.8 percent year-on-year. Exports of electric vehicles, lithium batteries and photovoltaic products -- often referred to as the "new trio" -- rose 27.1 percent. Wind turbine exports jumped 48.7 percent. For Li, those figures have a tangible counterpart: the equipment he now sees being loaded onto ships and sent to market thousands of kilometers from China. But the transformation of trade has come as the environment surrounding it has grown more difficult. The cargoes are changing. So is the environment in which they move. Karolina Czarnowska, a sales executive at Chipolbrok for four years, said geopolitical tensions have made international shipping increasingly unpredictable, while fuel prices can swing sharply. Much of her job involves visiting customers, listening to their needs and working with colleagues to find solutions. She said customers often point to that responsiveness as one of the company's strengths. In a volatile market, Czarnowska said, reliable end-to-end logistics services give customers greater confidence and have helped strengthen their trust in Chinese shipping companies. That experience has also shaped her view of Chinese businesses. "I believe they can survive and develop even in a difficult international environment," she said. The same uncertainty has also made international cooperation increasingly important in shipping. Chipolbrok began by linking China and Poland by sea. Over the decades, its services expanded far beyond bilateral trade, reaching markets across the world. In a message marking the company's 75th anniversary, Arkadiusz Marchewka, Deputy Minister of Polish Infrastructure Ministry, drew a parallel between shipping and economic cooperation. "At sea, success is never the work of one person alone," he said, adding that lasting partnerships likewise require common goals, professionalism and mutual respect. Czarnowska sees that cooperation in much more everyday terms. Chinese and Polish colleagues may have different ways of working and different ideas, she said, but those differences also give both sides opportunities to learn from one another. "You can always learn from the other side," she said. "Chinese colleagues have different ideas, and then together we can do something. It's very valuable." ■ A drone photo taken on Aug. 15, 2026 shows a new vessel undergoing sea trials jointly conducted by Chinese and Polish shipbuilding supervision teams in Nantong, east China's Jiangsu Province. (Chipolbrok/Handout via Xinhua)

Photograph: Joe Kline/AP Oregon Shooter kills three children and one teacher at Oregon elementary school Two people critical in hospital as officials in Bend say 16-year-old suspect shot dead by bystander Oregon elementary school shooting: what we know so far Uwa Ede-Osifo Thu 15 Oct 2026 21.53 EDT First published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 17.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 16-year-old shooter opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon , on Thursday, fatally shooting a teacher and three children before he was killed by a community member, authorities said at a evening news conference. The juvenile victims were five, eight and 11 years old, officials said. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old are also hospitalized with critical injuries, according to police. Oregon elementary school shooting: what we know so far Read more The gunman, who was a Bend resident, has not been publicly identified. Officials said they are still investigating if he had ties to Silver Rail elementary school. The deadly shooting has rocked the city of 100,000 residents located on the Deschutes River, roughly 170 miles south-east of Portland. “Please hold your children, hold your loved ones tight tonight. Let them talk. Let them cry. Let them know we are going to rally and care for one another in this community,” said Steven Cook, the superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools. “We will get through this – but not yet. We must grieve for the loss of our community members.” At 1.02pm, police responded to Silver Rail elementary school after receiving several reports about an active shooter. One 911 caller reported an individual armed with a long gun firing upon their car. Police did not specify the firearm’s make. Dozens of callers stated the shooter had entered the school, continuing the attack inside. He forced entry into the building by shooting at locked doors, according to police. By the time officers arrived on scene, the suspected assailant had been shot and killed by a bystander, who apprehended him inside. Oregon governor Tina Kotek praised the intervention as heroic and extended her thoughts to the bystander. “Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden,” she said on Thursday evening. The Bend-La Pine school district announced that its schools would be closed on Friday due to the tragedy. The FBI is helping local authorities investigate the shooting, according to the agency’s director Kash Patel. The shooting began about an hour before the school day was set to end. “A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure,” said Bend mayor Melanie Kebler. “Like so many in our community, I’m struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable.” Thursday’s shooting is the latest event in a grim history of recurring gun violence at schools across the US. According to Everytown For Gun Safety, there have been at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds across the country in 2026, resulting in 33 deaths. Oregon has passed several gun safety measures in recent years, including a law that requires gun owners to undergo a criminal background check and safety training before being approved for a firearm permit.
